title: Credential vs. Licensure vs. Program Completion

unit.title: Program Orientation, Professionalism, and Healthcare Roles

sections.learningObjectives:
- Distinguish program completion (certificate or degree), certification, registration, and licensure.
- Explain which organization or agency grants each type of credential.
- Recognize that credentialing requirements vary by employer and by state.
- Describe how medical assisting credentials are obtained and maintained.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

When you finish school, the school gives you a paper — a certificate, diploma, or degree — that says 'you finished.' It is like getting a trophy for completing a class, not a special permission slip to work.

### Question 2

The school is the one that hands out the 'you finished' paper. The state, the boss, and the exam groups each give out different kinds of papers later.

### Question 3

The AAMA is a group of medical assistants, and their special 'Certifying Board' gives out the CMA award after you pass a big test. It is like a club handing out a badge for members who prove they know the stuff.

### Question 4

The NHA is the group that gives out the CMAA badge after you pass a test about office and paperwork duties. It is a private group, not the government.

### Question 5

Only the government (your state) can give a license — the special permission that says you are legally allowed to do a certain job. Clubs and schools cannot hand out that permission.

### Question 6

Registration is like writing your name on a big official list so everyone can see who is allowed to be there. It is different from a diploma, a test badge, or just having a job.

### Question 7

A license is the biggest, strictest permission — like a driver's license you legally must have to drive. A certificate or test badge is helpful, but it is not the same as the law's permission.

### Question 8

Certification is like earning a special badge by passing a big test to show you know your stuff. You do not have to get the badge in most places, but many bosses like it.

### Question 9

The CMAA is the badge for the 'desk job' side of medical assisting — appointments, files, and patient information. The CMA badge covers a wider mix of clinical and desk work.

### Question 10

Before you can take the big AAMA test, you first have to finish an approved medical assisting school program. It is like needing to finish driving school before taking the road test.

### Question 11

Every five years, a CMA has to show they still know their stuff — by taking classes or a test again. It is like renewing a passport so it stays valid.

### Question 12

Finishing school gives you a 'you finished' paper. Certification gives you a 'you passed the test and really know it' badge. Two different papers!

### Question 13

Right after school you only have the 'you finished' paper. The CMA and CMAA badges come only after you pass their tests.

### Question 14

The state government gives out licenses (legal permission). Private clubs like the AAMA and NHA give out certification badges. Different givers, different papers.

### Question 15

In most states, a medical assistant does not need a special government license to work — though a few states do have extra rules. It depends on where you live.

### Question 16

The boss can ask for a badge even if the law does not. That is the boss's own rule, not the government's rule.

### Question 17

If the law says you need a license to do a job, doing it without one is against the law — like driving without a driver's license. No badge or boss's okay replaces it.

### Question 18

A degree is a fancy 'you finished college' paper from your school. It is not a license, not a test badge, and not a name on a list.

### Question 19

To keep your badge, you keep learning a little each year or retake the test sometimes. It is like keeping a garden growing so it does not dry up.

### Question 20

Three papers, three givers: the school gives the 'finished' paper, the club gives the test badge, and the state gives the license.

### Question 21

"Preferred" means the boss would really like it, like a restaurant that prefers diners make reservations — but you might still get a table. "Required" is the strict word.

### Question 22

Rules are different in different states, just like some states have different driving rules. Before you start, check the rules for your state.

### Question 23

Registration = writing your name on a list. Licensure = getting the law's permission to do the job. A list and a permission are not the same.

### Question 24

She finished school, so she has the 'finished' paper. But she has not passed the test, so she does not have the CMA badge yet.

### Question 25

Saying 'licensed by the AAMA' is like saying a scout club gave you a driver's license. Clubs give badges, not licenses.

### Question 26

If a patient asks, tell the truth simply: 'I have a certification badge, and in most states my job does not need a license.' Never pretend to be a doctor or to have a license you do not have.

### Question 27

The boss wants the CMAA badge, which comes from passing the NHA test about office work. So the new person needs to study and pass that test.

### Question 28

To take the AAMA test, your school must be on the special 'approved schools' list. If your school is not on the list, you cannot take the test yet.

### Question 29

The law might say 'you do not need a license,' but the boss can still say 'I want my workers to have the badge.' The boss can ask for more than the law asks.

### Question 30

Both people can legally do the job. The boss might like the one with the badge more, but the boss gets to choose — the law does not pick for them.

### Question 31

If the law says only a licensed person can do a job, you must say 'that is not for me' and tell your supervisor — even if a boss or a friend says to do it.

### Question 32

Every five years you refresh your learning so your knowledge stays sharp, like updating an app so it keeps working right.

### Question 33

If you stop taking your little learning classes, your badge can expire, like a gym membership you stop paying for. You have to keep it up yourself.

### Question 34

The school's 'you finished' paper is not the same as the 'you passed the big test' badge. One shows you finished; the other shows you proved your skills.

### Question 35

Each state makes its own rulebook, like each state having slightly different traffic rules. That is why the rules change when you cross a state line.

### Question 36

If a job posting says 'registered,' do not guess — look it up on the state's official website to see exactly what they mean. Guessing about rules is like guessing about a recipe.

### Question 37

The CMA badge shows you know both the desk work AND the exam-room work. The CMAA badge is mainly about the desk work.

### Question 38

The state's rule is like a law everyone must follow; the boss's rule is like a house rule at their own office. Sometimes both exist, but they come from different places.

### Question 39

A license is a law you must obey to do the job. A certification is a badge you choose to earn. Laws are stricter than choices.

### Question 40

To earn the AAMA badge, you must graduate from a school on the approved list. Working in an office or passing a different test does not count.

### Question 41

A list of people who are allowed to be called medical assistants is a 'registry.' Being on the list is registration, not a license or a test badge.

### Question 42

Even if you have a license, the boss can still say 'I also want my workers to have this badge.' The boss makes their own house rules.

### Question 43

First you finish school, then you take the big test. It is like finishing driving lessons before you take the road test.

### Question 44

The badge tells the boss 'this person passed a hard test and knows the job.' That is why bosses like it — it is proof, not a guess.

### Question 45

If you ever need a license, it comes from the state government. The badges come from the clubs, and the 'finished' paper comes from your school.

### Question 46

The new medical assisting certificate is the 'you finished this program' paper. The old degree is a different paper from before.

### Question 47

The big test checks whether you really know the job before the AAMA hands you the badge. It is a 'prove it' test.

### Question 48

The CMAA badge is made exactly for desk-and-paperwork jobs like scheduling and records. It is the right badge for this kind of work.

### Question 49

Two rulebooks can both apply: the state's law book and the boss's house rules. They are separate and can say different things.

### Question 50

Every five years, you show you are still up to date — like passing a small check-up test to keep your badge shiny.

### Question 51

Rules change when you cross a state line. Before doing a task in a new state, check that state's rulebook first.

### Question 52

Pick the badge that matches your dream job: the wide badge (CMA) for clinical plus desk work, or the desk badge (CMAA) for office work.

### Question 53

Your school gives you the diploma. The state gives licenses, and the clubs give badges. The diploma is the school's gift.

### Question 54

Being 'on the list' before doing a task is registration. It is the state checking off your name, not giving you a badge or a license.

### Question 55

A certification is a badge from a club; a license is permission from the government. Clubs give badges, governments give licenses.

### Question 56

Both badges are optional and show you know your stuff, but they come from two different clubs and focus on slightly different jobs.

### Question 57

A badge shows you know how, but the law might still say only a licensed person may do it. Knowing how and having permission are two different things.

### Question 58

The school paper says 'you finished the classes.' The badges say 'you passed the big test.' The school paper alone does not prove the test.

### Question 59

The law sets the lowest bar, but a boss can raise their own bar higher. It is like a store allowing returns for 30 days but choosing to offer 90.

### Question 60

The CMAA badge tells the boss 'this person knows office work.' It is a proof-of-knowledge badge, not a license or a degree.

### Question 61

Only say 'certified' if you have a badge, and only say 'licensed' if the government gave you a license. Words about credentials must be true.

### Question 62

When the state says 'you must pass this test first,' that is a law, not a suggestion.

### Question 63

The school paper is the easiest step — it just shows you finished. The badges, lists, and licenses all add more rules on top.

### Question 64

Saying you have a license when you do not is like saying you won a race you did not run. It is not true, and people trust you less when they find out.

### Question 65

If you are not sure a task is allowed, ask and check the rules first — like checking a map before taking a turn. Do not just guess.

### Question 66

If you see someone doing a job they are not allowed to do, tell the boss quietly. Do not start a fight and do not copy them.

### Question 67

'Contingent' means 'only if.' The job is yours only if you earn the badge in time.

### Question 68

If a patient asks for doctor-style advice, kindly say 'that is a question for your provider' and point them to the right person. Do not pretend to be a doctor.

### Question 69

Most states do not make the badge a law. A few places have extra rules, and some bosses require it — but 'everyone must have it by law' is not true.

### Question 70

When the rules are fuzzy, ask the rule-makers or your supervisor — do not guess and do not sneak.

### Question 71

When a practice says its workers are 'certified,' it usually means they earned a badge like the CMA or CMAA. It is a boast about training and tests.

### Question 72

Finishing school teaches you the job, but the law decides what you are allowed to do. The school paper is not a permission slip from the law.

### Question 73

If your badge expires, tell the boss right away and work to get it back. Do not pretend it is still good.

### Question 74

A national badge travels with you like a library card that works in many places, while a license is like a driver's license from one state.

### Question 75

Doing a job that only licensed people may do is stepping outside your lane. Staying in your lane means doing the tasks your badge and the law allow.

### Question 76

Two papers, two achievements: one says 'I finished school,' the other says 'I passed the big test.' Both belong on your resume.

### Question 77

Tell patients the simple truth: 'I passed a big national test that shows I know medical assisting.' That is clear and honest.

### Question 78

Different states have different laws, and different bosses have different rules — that is why there is no one-size-fits-all answer.

### Question 79

If a new job task shows up, ask your supervisor what training and permission are needed before you start — like checking you have the right gear before a hike.

### Question 80

If a state calls you 'registered,' it means your name is on their official list. Check that state's rules to see exactly how to get on the list.

### Question 81

When you are unsure and the rulebook is quiet, ask your supervisor and check the official rules. Do not guess.

### Question 82

A badge is only worth what people think of the club that gave it. A badge from a well-known, trusted club is worth more.

### Question 83

The boss checks your badge is still fresh so everyone on the team stays sharp and legal — like a coach checking players' equipment.

### Question 84

If someone asks about the rules and you are not sure, say 'I am not sure — check the state's official website.' Guessing about rules is like guessing the answer on a test you did not study for.
